notable_claims: The university's threat of investigation for continued complaints constitutes a 'chilling effect' on student speech.
Threatening students with expulsion processes can be compared to the irreparable harm caused by the Un-American Activities Committee.
classification.summary: Howard Goldstein critiques Carnegie Mellon University's handling of a student's speech, arguing that the university's threat of investigation creates a 'chilling effect.' He contends that conditional forbearance by the administration acts as a form of harassment against the student. Goldstein suggests that shielding students from offensive speech in an academic setting is ethically irresponsible.
classification.title: Speech Restrictions On Cm

notable_claims: CMU's administration suggested an inquiry that could curtail a student's academic endeavors due to bulletin board posts.
The author claims the university is using 'harassment' as a pretext to censor offensive speech in a public forum.
classification.summary: Robert F. Solon criticizes Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) for potential censorship of a user who posted allegedly harassing messages on a public bulletin board. Solon argues that the university's actions prioritize protecting individuals from offense over the free exchange of ideas and the search for truth. He contends that users can simply ignore offensive posts, making the 'harassment' claim invalid.
classification.title: Re: Speech restrictions on CMU computers

identity.subject: Re: Speech restrictions on CMU computers

notable_claims: Courts in Doe v. U. of Michigan and UWM Post v. U. of Wisconsin found that prohibitions on certain types of speech at state schools are not justified.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie responds to John Gardiner Myers regarding the justification for prohibiting 'discriminatory speech' on university computer systems. Kadie cites legal precedents from state schools to argue that such prohibitions are not legally justified.
classification.title: Speech restrictions on CMU computer bboards

identity.subject: Re: Speech restrictions on CMU computer bboards

notable_claims: CMU systems (MacMail, EZ Mail, and AMS) allow users to skim subject headers before reading messages.
classification.summary: A response to a debate regarding speech and harassment on Carnegie Mellon University's electronic bulletin boards. The author argues that because email and board software allow users to screen subject headers, the responsibility for avoiding offensive content lies with the reader rather than through administrative restriction.
classification.title: Speech restrictions on CMU computer bboards

identity.subject: Re: Speech restrictions on CMU computer bboards

notable_claims: Suppression of expression based on subjective definitions of harassment is a 'slippery slope'.
The search for truth in academic institutions is compromised when any form of expression is suppressed.
classification.summary: Robert F. Solon argues against the suppression of intimidating or harassing speech at Carnegie Mellon University, claiming that such restrictions are subjective and compromise the search for truth. He contends that education is a better alternative to censorship and warns that imposing ideological conformity mirrors totalitarian regimes.
classification.title: The Dark Ages Revisited (Was Re: Supression on speech on CM)

notable_claims: The distinction between 'offensive' and 'harassing' speech is being used to suppress speech that is merely offensive.
Speech on a bulletin board cannot be considered harassment if the reader can easily ignore it or if no specific individuals are targeted.
classification.summary: Christian M. Restifo challenges the justification for restricting speech on Carnegie Mellon University's electronic bulletin boards. He argues against the classification of offensive or general derogatory speech as 'harassment,' questioning how such content causes real harm in a digital environment where users can ignore messages.
classification.title: Speech restrictions on CMU computer bboards

notable_claims: The updated fingerd program on uxa returns legal names regardless of user preference.
Forcing the display of legal names violates the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act of 1974.
classification.summary: Michael D. Adams sent a formal complaint to the Director of the Computing Services Office at UIUC regarding a software update to the 'fingerd' program on the uxa mainframe. The update forced the display of users' legal names, removing the ability for individuals to customize or suppress their identity. Adams argues this change violates University policy and the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) of 1974.
classification.title: Complaint letter about fingerd change

notable_claims: CCSO believes perceived anonymity leads to increased belligerence and decreased responsibility.
The 'uxa' account service is not mandated by the University and receives no funding from the computer fee committee.
CCSO may stop providing general student accounts if courts rule against the disclosure of student names.
organizations: University of Illinois Computing Services Office
classification.summary: Steve Dorner of UIUC's Computing Services Office (CCSO) defends the decision to identify users on the network via fingerd to reduce belligerence and increase accountability. He discusses the tension between user privacy rights under the Privacy Act and the optional nature of 'uxa' accounts provided by CCSO. Dorner suggests that if legal mandates prevent identification, CCSO may cease providing general student accounts entirely.
classification.title: Re: an open letter to the cso.gods

identity.subject: Re: an open letter to the cso.gods

notable_claims: Institutions may not require a waiver of FERPA rights as a condition for admission or receipt of services.
Directory information is defined as data that would not be considered harmful or an invasion of privacy if disclosed.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie questions whether a university can legally condition the provision of services, specifically computer accounts and email access, on a student's agreement to release directory information. He cites FERPA regulations and legal compendiums to explore the boundaries between privacy rights and institutional requirements.
classification.title: Requiring students to release directory information

identity.subject: Requiring students to release directory information

notable_claims: The University of Oregon's de facto news policy was to carry anything legal.
NewsWatcher for Mac had a 32K character limit for its .newsrc equivalent, necessitating the filtering of newsgroups.
classification.summary: JQ Johnson of the University of Oregon discusses the institution's policy of carrying all legal newsgroups, except for restricted-distribution hierarchies. He notes that while disk space was previously managed via expiration dates, a technical limitation in the NewsWatcher software for Mac forced the university to manually trim the list of available groups. This created a conflict between maintaining broad access and supporting specific user agent constraints.
classification.title: Usenet News Selection Policies
